overview:
Rwanda is a small, green, steeply folded country in the heart of East Africa, landlocked between Uganda, Tanzania, Burundi, and the Democratic Republic of the Congo. About the size of Maryland, it is one of the most densely populated countries in Africa, with roughly 14 million people farming terraced slopes that earn it the nickname land of a thousand hills.

Kinyarwanda is spoken by nearly everyone, and English and French are official languages too. Kigali, the capital, spreads across several ridges and is known around the continent for its clean, orderly streets; plastic bags are banned nationwide, and on the last Saturday of each month neighbors turn out for umuganda, a morning of shared community work.

Rwanda is a republic with an elected president. Coffee, tea, and visitors who come to track mountain gorillas are its main earners, and the country has rebuilt determinedly since the genocide of 1994.
landAndNature: Rwanda sits high, mostly between 1,000 and 4,500 meters, so even on the edge of the equator the air stays mild and evenings turn cool. Volcanoes rise along the northern border as part of the Virunga chain, where Karisimbi reaches 4,507 meters and bamboo forest shelters roughly a third of the world's remaining mountain gorillas. Nyungwe Forest in the southwest is one of Africa's oldest rainforests, full of chimpanzees, colobus monkeys, and orchids, with a walkway slung across the treetops. Akagera National Park in the east holds swamps and savanna where lions and rhinos have been returned after years away. Lake Kivu fills a deep valley on the Congolese border.
peopleAndCulture: Rwandans share a single language and many traditions across the groups known as Hutu, Tutsi, and Twa; since 1994 the government has emphasized one common Rwandan identity. Most people are Christian. Meals are built on beans, plantains, cassava, sweet potatoes, and isombe, a stew of pounded cassava leaves. Imigongo art covers wooden boards with bold black, white, and red geometric patterns. The intore dance, once performed for kings, has men in long grass headdresses leaping to the beat of drums. Tightly woven baskets with peaked lids, called agaseke, are given as wedding gifts. Cycling is the national sporting passion, and the Tour du Rwanda climbs those endless hills.
history: Twa hunter-gatherers, then farmers and cattle herders, settled these hills, and by the 1700s a strong kingdom ruled from the center under a mwami, or king. Germany claimed Rwanda in the 1890s, and Belgium took over after World War I, hardening the divide between Hutu and Tutsi with identity cards. Independence came on July 1, 1962, followed by decades of ethnic violence and waves of refugees. In 1994, over about a hundred days, extremist forces and militias killed around 800,000 people, most of them Tutsi along with moderate Hutu, in a genocide that the outside world watched without intervening. A rebel army ended the killing that July. Rwanda has since concentrated on justice, reconciliation, and rebuilding.
funFacts: Rwanda banned plastic bags in 2008, and airport officials still take them from arriving travelers' luggage.
Rwanda's parliament has one of the highest shares of women in the world, with more than half its lower house.
Drones launched from Rwandan bases deliver blood to remote hospitals by parachute, a service started in 2016.
Mountain gorilla numbers have climbed back above a thousand, and every new gorilla baby is named at a public ceremony.
Kigali sits just south of the equator but rarely gets hot, because the whole city stands about 1,500 meters above sea level.
